analysis.one_liner: Strips federal tax breaks from corporations that run private prisons.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Finance Committee, where it never advanced before the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Two large private prison companies reorganized themselves as real estate investment trusts (REITs), a tax structure meant for landlords and hotels, which let them avoid paying corporate income taxes. This bill would change the tax code so that any corporation operating or managing a prison, or licensing a prison brand, could no longer qualify as a REIT subsidiary. The companies would then owe standard corporate taxes on their profits.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal and state taxpayers, who would collect corporate taxes from private prison companies that currently avoid them. It also would remove a tax incentive that rewards the private prison business model, in which companies profit from filling beds at jails and detention centers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the tax code to exclude any corporation that operates or manages a prison facility, or provides services at one, from the definition of a taxable REIT subsidiary, ending their ability to use that structure [S2] [S3].
It also covers companies that license prison brands to operators, closing a route around the rule, and it defines 'prison facility' as any correctional, detention, or penal facility [S3].
The change applies to tax years starting after enactment, so it would take effect immediately if passed [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The private prison companies themselves, chiefly CoreCivic (formerly Corrections Corporation of America) and GEO Group, which reorganized as REITs in 2013 and have since paid little or no corporate income tax. Prison operators would either pay standard corporate taxes or restructure.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not shut down private prisons or reduce incarceration; it only removes a tax preference, so companies could still profit from running prisons while paying normal corporate taxes.

The private prison industry argues its REIT structure follows the tax code as written, since prison operators lease and manage facilities much like hotel landlords; the bill is effectively a targeted rewrite of the rule for one industry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is narrow but straightforward: it closes a tax shelter that was never meant to cover prisons, and the main cost falls on two companies whose business model profits from incarceration. Its limits are real — it does nothing about the contracts or the practice of private prisons themselves — but its aim, restoring tax revenue from prison companies, is clearly served.

outcome.mechanism: Wyden introduced the bill and it was sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator Ron Wyden introduced the bill on July 14, 2016, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1] [S5].
No senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The Finance Committee took no further action, and the bill died there when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The private prison companies keep their REIT status and the accompanying tax savings. Taxpayers continue to forgo the corporate tax revenue those companies would otherwise pay.

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-OR), bill sponsor and member of the Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee, on which he sits

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for committee action, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew no cosponsors at all — none from Democrats and none from Republicans — so no party bloc ever took a position on the record [S4].

industries.note: Companies like CoreCivic and GEO Group reorganized as REITs in 2013, a structure meant for hotels and landlords, and have largely avoided corporate income tax since. This bill would end that break, raising their tax bills while they continue to profit from holding inmates at per-bed rates. Their interest in keeping the tax structure runs against taxpayers' interest in collecting the revenue.

The REIT tax structure itself would remain untouched; only prison operators would be excluded from using it. The broader REIT industry would be unaffected, though the bill signals that Congress can bar industries it dislikes from the structure.
